opus-5.5.text:
I think that argument is partly right, but the framing of "first real, then synthetic" is too sequential. In practice the two have to grow together.

Here's the part I agree with. Synthetic data is only as good as the model of the world that generates it. If your simulator gets contact dynamics, friction, deformable objects, or sensor noise wrong, the policy learns to exploit those errors, and then it falls apart on a real table. So you need real data to know where the simulator is lying to you. Without that anchor you can generate billions of trajectories and still be optimizing in the wrong universe. Real data plays the role of calibration and ground truth.

Where I disagree is the idea that you need some huge threshold of real data before synthetic data becomes useful. That isn't what we've seen. Locomotion is the clearest counterexample. Quadrupeds and now humanoids learned robust walking almost entirely in simulation with domain randomization, plus a fairly small amount of real-world tuning. For tasks where the physics is well understood and the main difficulty is control, synthetic data was useful from day one.

Manipulation is harder, because the bottleneck is less about physics and more about the long tail of objects, scenes, and human intentions. Even there, synthetic data helps early on visual diversity, task variations, failure cases you'd never want to collect on a real robot, and pre-training representations. It just can't carry the whole load on its own.

So I'd describe it as a loop rather than a ladder. You collect some real data and find where your policy fails. You use that to improve your simulator or generative world model. You generate a lot of targeted synthetic data around those gaps, deploy, and collect again. Each turn of the loop makes the real data more valuable, because it's spent on the hard cases, and makes the synthetic data more trustworthy, because it's been checked against reality.

There's also an economic point. Real robot data is expensive and slow. Teleoperation hours don't scale like internet text. If the whole field waited until it had "enough" real data, we might wait a very long time. The teams that move fastest will treat real data as the scarce, high-value signal and use synthetic data and video world models as the multiplier.

So my short answer: real data is necessary, but it isn't a prerequisite stage you have to finish first. It's the compass, and synthetic data is the engine. You need both running at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response says teleoperation hours are expensive and do not scale like internet text, but it does not say teleoperation-based solutions must establish a positive business loop before scaling.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that argument gets the order roughly right but draws the line in the wrong place. It's not that real data comes first and then synthetic data becomes useful. It's that the two have to grow together, and the question is always: what is the synthetic data being grounded in?

Let me explain why I see it that way. In language, the internet gave you a free prior. Models learned what the world looks like from text before anyone tried to generate more text. Robotics has no equivalent. There is no "internet of robot actions." So when people say we need real-world data first, what they really mean is we need a seed that captures the physical world's actual distribution: how objects deform, how contact behaves, how lighting shifts, how a gripper slips. If you skip that and go straight to simulation, you end up generating enormous volumes of data about a world that doesn't exist, and the model becomes very confident about the wrong physics.

But I'd push back on the idea that there's some threshold you cross and then synthetic data switches on. In practice, the real data's value is not just volume. It's coverage and calibration. A few thousand carefully collected trajectories that span the hard cases can anchor a simulator or a world model far better than a million repetitive demonstrations of the same pick-and-place. And once you have that anchor, synthetic data does something real data can't do cheaply: it lets you explore failure modes, rare conditions, and long-tail combinations you would never collect by hand.

So the loop I believe in looks like this. Collect real data deliberately, use it to validate and correct your generative pipeline, generate synthetic data at scale, train, then deploy and collect more real data specifically where the model fails. Real data tells you where your synthetic world is lying to you. Synthetic data tells you where to send your real-world collection budget next.

The companies that treat it as a sequential pipeline, real first and synthetic later, tend to get stuck either collecting forever or simulating something nobody can transfer. The ones treating it as a closed loop, where each side keeps correcting the other, are the ones actually making progress.

r001.rationale: The response describes a feedback loop between real and synthetic data, but does not state that teleoperation-based robotics solutions need a positive business loop before scaling.

astra-6.text:
I think that argument is too absolute. You need some real-world data to understand what matters and to check whether your simulation captures it. But that’s different from saying you must accumulate a huge amount before synthetic data becomes useful.

The key question is: useful for what? If you’re learning visual recognition or testing planning strategies, synthetic data can help quite early. If you’re learning delicate contact—how an object slips, how much force to apply—the gap between simulation and reality becomes more consequential.

I’d treat it as a loop. Collect some real data, identify where the model fails, use simulation to generate relevant variations, and then test again in the real world. Real data helps you improve the synthetic data, and synthetic data can help you make better use of the real data.

So I wouldn’t set a universal threshold for how much real data you need. I’d ask whether adding synthetic data improves performance on real tasks. That’s the test that matters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how real and synthetic data can complement each other, but does not mention teleoperation-based solutions, a positive business loop, or scaling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that argument is too absolute. Some real-world data is important, but I don’t think there’s a threshold you have to cross before synthetic data suddenly becomes useful. The question is what you’re trying to learn and how well your simulation captures the things that matter for that task.

For example, synthetic data can help a robot learn to recognize objects under different lighting conditions or practice reaching for objects in different positions. Contact-rich manipulation is harder, because friction, deformation, and small physical differences can change the outcome. In those cases, real-world data becomes especially valuable for identifying what the simulation is missing.

So I would treat this as an iterative process: use real-world experiments to ground the simulation, use simulation to explore more broadly, then test the results in the real world. You don’t necessarily need a huge amount of real data to begin. You need enough relevant evidence to know whether the synthetic data is actually helping.

r001.rationale: The response discusses real-world and synthetic data in robotics, but it does not mention teleoperation-based solutions, a positive business loop, or scaling.
